opening_note: October in San Diego doesn't look like fall; some of the year's hottest days land this month. But the evenings shorten, the squash gets sweeter, the last poblanos are going, and at some point you'll want the oven on. This edition is about that moment.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

weekend_meal.label: The featured cook
weekend_meal.name: Dutch-oven chicken with delicata and white beans.
weekend_meal.intro: The whole month in one pot, and the braise that teaches you the rest.
weekend_meal.card_line: Chicken thighs, delicata, white beans, poblano, rosemary, lemon
weekend_meal.time: About an hour and a quarter, twenty minutes of it active. Serves four, with lunch left over.
ingredients: 6 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs, about 2½ lbs
1 delicata squash — halved, seeded, cut into 1-inch half-moons, skin on
2 poblanos, seeded and cut into strips
2 cans cannellini beans, drained and rinsed
2 cups chicken stock, or 2 tsp bouillon in 2 cups hot water
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: Salt the chicken the night before, or an hour ahead, if you remember. If you don't, salt it right before. It still works.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 375°F. Pat the chicken dry and salt both sides. Set the Dutch oven over medium-high with a thin film of oil and lay the thighs in skin side down — in two batches if they crowd. Leave them alone for 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and lets go of the pot on its own. Turn them for two minutes, then move them to a plate. Pour off all but about two tablespoons of fat.
Turn the heat to medium. Add the poblano, garlic, and rosemary to the fat and stir for three or four minutes, until the chile softens and the kitchen smells like it.
Pour in a splash of the stock and scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon. The brown layer stuck to the pot is the most flavorful thing in it. It belongs in the sauce, not in the sink.

Add the beans, the squash, and the rest of the stock. Season with salt and pepper. Nestle the chicken back in, skin side up. The liquid should come about halfway up the thighs, with the skin above it.
Into the oven, lid off, for 45 minutes. Below the surface everything turns to stew; above it, the skin crisps again. It's done when the squash is tender and the meat pulls from the bone.
Zest the lemon over the pot, then squeeze in half of it. Taste the beans and salt them if they need it. Let it sit ten minutes. Serve from the pot, with bread for the liquid.

after.heading: The next day
after.body: Pull the chicken off the bone and stir it back into the beans. Warm it with a splash of water, or eat it at room temperature over rice or toast with the other half of the lemon. It's better on Monday.

delicata-squash.name: Delicata squash
delicata-squash.tile_uses: Roasted, the braise, pasta, beside salmon
delicata-squash.why_now: September brought the first ones. By October they've cured longer — more orange down in the grooves, sweeter inside — and they cost less. It's the squash in the Sunday braise, and the one worth keeping two of on the counter all month.
how_to_choose: Orange in the grooves between the green stripes means longer cured and sweeter
Heavy for its size and firm at both ends
Small to medium; the big ones get watery
delicata-squash.buy_this_much: 3. Two for roasting through the week, one for the pot on Sunday.
weekday_uses: Roasted beside salmon on the same sheet pan
Folded into pasta with butter browned with sage
Cold from the fridge in a rice bowl, with pomegranate
In the Dutch oven with chicken and white beans
delicata-squash.storage: On the counter, out of the sun, for a month. It doesn't want the fridge. Once cut, wrap it and use it within four days.
delicata-squash.one_thing_to_learn: Delicata holds its shape in a braise where butternut would collapse. The thin skin you don't peel is structure. For the pot, cut it thick — an inch — so it turns tender when the chicken does, not before.
delicata-squash.market_question: Which of these has been curing longest?

poblanos.name: The last poblanos

default_move.headline: Char it. You already know how.

poblanos.tile_uses: The braise, rice bowls, tacos, the freezer
poblanos.why_now: Roasting chiles run from late August to about mid-October, then they're gone until next year. The ones still around this month are often blushing red, a little sweeter and sometimes a little hotter. Buy them now; they freeze better than almost anything.
how_to_choose: Glossy and heavy, with no wrinkles
A red blush means riper — sweeter, and sometimes hotter
poblanos.buy_this_much: 4–6. Two go into the braise raw. Char the rest and freeze the strips for November.
weekday_uses: Sliced raw into the braise with the garlic
Charred strips in a ground-beef rice bowl
In tacos with roasted sweet potato
Chopped into scrambled eggs
poblanos.storage: Raw, a week in the crisper. Charred and peeled, four days in the fridge — or freeze the strips flat in a bag and break off what you need.
poblanos.one_thing_to_learn: Raw poblano and charred poblano are two different vegetables. Sliced raw and cooked in fat, it's green and grassy, doing what a bell pepper does with more to say. Charred, it's smoky and soft. The braise wants the first. The rice bowl wants the second.
poblanos.market_question: How many more weeks of these?

sweet-potatoes.name: Sweet potatoes

default_move.headline: Cut side down. Don't flip it.
steps: cut side down on the pan

sweet-potatoes.why_now: Most of California's sweet potatoes come out of the ground around Merced in September and October. The new crop is on the shelves now — at its cheapest, and not yet tired from months in storage.
how_to_choose: Firm all over, with no soft ends and no sprouts
Medium and even in shape, so they cook at one speed
sweet-potatoes.buy_this_much: 2 lbs. They keep, so they're the thing you cook the week it gets away from you.
weekday_uses: Cut side down beside pork chops
Cubed and roasted into tacos with poblano and pomegranate
In a rice bowl with ground beef
Split open with yogurt, salt, and chile
sweet-potatoes.storage: Somewhere cool and dark, not the fridge — cold turns the center hard and odd-tasting. They keep for weeks.
sweet-potatoes.one_thing_to_learn: Cut side down is the whole trick. The flat face sits on the hot pan and the sugars caramelize into a dark crust while the inside steams in its own skin. Flip it halfway and you lose the crust. Leave it alone.

apples.name: Late Julian apples

default_move.headline: Now you can cook them.
steps: into the pan after the pork

apples.why_now: September's apples were for eating raw. October's are Julian's late ones — Granny Smith, Pink Lady, Winesap — tarter and firmer, which is exactly what you want in a hot pan. They hold their shape next to pork instead of turning to sauce.
how_to_choose: Firm, with no give near the stem
Tart varieties for the pan; sweet ones for eating
The blossom end should smell like apple
apples.buy_this_much: 4–6. Two for the pan, the rest for eating. Buy them weekly; crisp is the point.
weekday_uses: In the pan after pork chops, with sage
Sliced thin into a slaw with pomegranate and cider vinegar
Grated over yogurt
With sharp cheddar and sourdough
apples.storage: In the fridge, away from anything that absorbs smells. Cold, they stay crisp for weeks.
apples.one_thing_to_learn: A cooking apple is just a tart, firm one. Sugar makes an apple collapse under heat; acid and density hold it together. That's why September said don't bake them yet, and October says go ahead.
apples.market_question: Which of these holds up in a pan?

pomegranates.name: Pomegranates
pomegranates.tile_uses: Over squash, rice bowls, tacos, slaw
pomegranates.why_now: Southern California grows pomegranates, and they ripen in October and November. A heavy one bought now keeps for weeks and turns anything rich into something brighter.
how_to_choose: Heavy for its size — weight is juice
Slightly angular, flat-sided shapes are the fullest
Taut, leathery skin; a dry crack is fine
pomegranates.buy_this_much: 2. One pomegranate is about a cup of seeds, which is a week of scattering.
weekday_uses: Over roasted delicata, while it's still hot
On a ground-beef rice bowl
On sweet potato tacos
Over yogurt with honey
pomegranates.storage: Whole, a month in the fridge. Seeded, five days in a covered container.
pomegranates.one_thing_to_learn: Pomegranate is October's lime: something sharp to put against heavier food. Rich things need acid — lemon in the braise, cider vinegar in the pork pan, pomegranate on the squash. Same move, different ingredient. Once you see it, you'll reach for it without thinking.

fuyu-persimmons.name: Fuyu persimmons

default_move.headline: Eat it firm, like an apple.

fuyu-persimmons.tile_uses: Sliced raw, with cheese, beside pork
fuyu-persimmons.why_now: Fuyus come from North County groves, usually in the last weeks of the month — so don't go looking on the first. When they turn up, they're one of the best things in the store, and almost nobody knows what to do with them.
how_to_choose: Squat and flat on top, shaped like a tomato — that's a Fuyu
Deep orange, firm but not rock hard
Tall and acorn-shaped is a Hachiya: leave it until it's soft as jelly
weekday_uses: Sliced into rounds with pomegranate and a little salt
With cheese, instead of an apple
Alongside pork chops
Diced over yogurt
fuyu-persimmons.storage: On the counter until they give very slightly, then the fridge for a week or two.
fuyu-persimmons.one_thing_to_learn: The two persimmons in the bin are not interchangeable. A firm Hachiya is so tannic it dries out your whole mouth; it has to go completely soft first. A Fuyu has no such problem and is good crisp. Learn the shape and you'll never make the mistake.
